title: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard -- Ch. 2: A Friendly Court
keywords: grumpy old men with failing eyesights
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- CJP's short welcome remarks at the ceremonies honoring the retiring Chief Justice, built on the contrast between the Court's remote, mysterious public face and the rare human, even friendly, face it shows on such occasions.

The portrait of how court watchers and even lawyers perceive the Supreme Court: an unsolvable puzzle inside a riddle, a collection of grumpy old men, a deity on Mt. Olympus that receives petitions and issues promulgations after an unpredictable lapse of time.

The description of the ceremonial exception -- scarlet-lined togas instead of dull all-black working robes, frowns replaced by smiles and waves, justices descending from their Olympian thrones to speak at microphones normally reserved for mere lawyers -- offered as proof that the Court is not just human but uncharacteristically friendly.

The occasion's double character: unusual because it honors the Chief himself, yet traditional because it follows familiar numbered sequences culled from a century of usage, and meant to proclaim both his virtues and the collective achievements of the Court he headed for seven years.
sub_topics: The opening image of the Court as an unsolvable puzzle contained in a riddle shrouded in mystery and imbedded in an enigma, whose mystic ways and traditions court watchers cannot penetrate even while appreciating its role as protector of the Constitution.

The public's picture of magistrates as grumpy old men with failing eyesights, unrecognizable on television or in the newspapers, so low-profile they cannot be picked out in a tapestry of common mortals.

The counterpoint that they are not ordinary mortals, since their decisions speak of precedence and continuity bordering on eternity, as if the writers had been with the Court since its birth almost a century ago.

The lawyers' experience of the Court: distant, impregnable and impersonal, an abstraction receiving petitions, supplications and prayers and issuing promulgations and commandments, which emerges from its hidden fortress at oral arguments only to mystify with hostile and perplexing questions before valued clients.

The ceremonial reversal: ceremonial togas, discarded frowns, nods and little-finger waves of recognition to friendly faces, and the descent from the rostrum -- noted in passing as having no front exit -- to the lawyers' microphones.
The framing of the day's ceremonies as a welcome respite, unusual in honoring the Chief but traditional in its century-old sequences.
The Tagalog welcome inviting the honored guests and friends to come in and join the joyful celebration for the Chief Justice.
The closing invitation to sit easy, relax and smile, with the observation that this is one time in the intimidating and cavernous hall when the audience may even applaud.

Indeed, this afternoon the Court is not just human. It is uncharacteristically friendly.
Mga pinagpipitagang panauhin at kaibigan, tuloy po kayo at makiisa sa aming maligayang pagbubunyi sa ating Punong Mahistrado.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' is Panganiban's brief welcome at the ceremonies honoring the retiring Chief Justice, and it turns on a single contrast. Court watchers, he observes, have compared the Supreme Court to an unsolvable puzzle contained in a riddle shrouded in mystery and imbedded in an enigma: they may appreciate its role as protector of the Constitution and defender of the people's liberties, but they find its mystic ways impenetrable and often picture its members as a collection of grumpy old men with failing eyesights, so low-profile that they cannot be picked out in a tapestry of common mortals. Yet ordinary mortals they are not, he says, because their decisions speak of precedence and continuity bordering on eternity, as though their authors had been with the Court since its birth almost a century earlier. Even to lawyers the Court is distant, impregnable and impersonal, an abstraction on Mt. Olympus that receives petitions, supplications and prayers and, after an unpredictable lapse, issues promulgations and commandments; in the one percent of the time it emerges from its hidden fortress for oral arguments, it mystifies counsel with hostile and perplexing questions before their valued clients. Retirement ceremonies are the exception. The justices exchange their dull all-black working robes for scarlet-lined ceremonial togas, discard their impatient frowns, nod and wave in recognition of friendly faces, and come down from their Olympian thrones to speak at microphones normally reserved for mere lawyers. The day's proceedings, he adds, are unusual because they honor the Chief himself but traditional because they follow familiar numbered sequences culled from a century of usage, and the Court has every reason to be friendly because it is proclaiming both its leader's virtues and the collective achievements of the seven years he headed it. He welcomes the guests in Tagalog and closes by inviting them to sit easy, relax, smile, and for once even applaud.
